summary: Provides a discussion of the protocols and techniques used to carry OSI CLNS and LLC1 datagrams on Network Systems Corporation's HYPERchannel equipment. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: It explains how to send one kind of network message over a particular company's fast cable system.

questions: how to run osi clns over hyperchannel
how do you send osi messages on hyperchannel
what is the hyperchannel message format
how do you run is-is on hyperchannel
subtitle: Running OSI protocols on Network Systems HYPERchannel equipment.

tldr.problem: Network Systems Corporation's HYPERchannel is a high-speed network technology that lacks broadcast capability, yet OSI protocols like ES-IS and IS-IS require it. Organizations needed a standard way to carry OSI traffic on HYPERchannel equipment.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines how to encapsulate LLC1 (a data link protocol) packets over HYPERchannel messages, specifying the message format with a 16-byte header. For protocols that require broadcasting, it describes emulation techniques: systems maintain lists of peers and send individual copies of packets to each one.
tldr.outcome: This enables organizations to run OSI protocols on HYPERchannel networks by providing clear standards for encapsulation and broadcast emulation, though it is limited to informational status and reflects an era when HYPERchannel and OSI were active technologies.

facts.label: Associated data limit
facts.value: Unlimited on HYPERchannel-50; 4 KB on HYPERchannel-10

today: RFC 1223 is an Informational RFC and has not been updated. It describes how to run OSI protocols on HYPERchannel, both of which are now legacy technologies. The content remains accurate for anyone working with historical HYPERchannel or OSI systems, but new networks today use different technologies.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Network Systems Corporation's HYPERchannel is a high-speed network technology designed for data transfer between systems. Unlike standard networks, HYPERchannel splits its messages into two parts: a small message header (16 to 64 bytes) that travels quickly and optionally a data section that follows at high speed. This design allows HYPERchannel to send control information rapidly while streaming large data blocks efficiently.

The RFC establishes how to carry OSI protocols, particularly CLNP (Connectionless Network Protocol) and LLC1 (a data link layer standard), on HYPERchannel equipment. OSI is a comprehensive suite of network protocols that were important in the 1980s and 1990s. Three main goals are addressed: standardizing the encapsulation of LLC1 packets, handling protocols that require broadcasting on a medium that does not naturally support it, and assigning protocol type numbers to different OSI protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: Network Systems made a very fast cable system. This document explains how to send a certain type of network message (called OSI messages) through that cable, and how to label the messages so the equipment knows what to do with them.

sections.title: HYPERchannel Message Structure
sections.content:
A HYPERchannel network message has two parts. The Message Proper is a fixed header of 16 to 64 bytes. The first 16 bytes contain delivery information: addresses, port numbers, and control flags. The remaining bytes (if any) are available for higher-level protocol information. The Associated Data section, which is optional, holds the actual payload. On HYPERchannel-50 (the main variant), the associated data can be very large, while on HYPERchannel-10 or within local adapters it is limited to 4 kilobytes.

The 16-byte delivery header includes the destination address (domain, network, unit), source address, a message type field (bytes 8 and 9), flags including whether associated data is present, and fields that help the network adapt to the message. A special flag called A/D (Associated Data Present) tells the hardware whether data follows the header. When only a message header is sent without data, HYPERchannel uses fast, abbreviated protocols and queuing. When data is included, the adapters coordinate their activities to stream data continuously at maximum speed.
sections.plainLanguage: A HYPERchannel message is like a postcard with an address label and an attached box for the real message. The label is always there, but the box is optional. If there is no box, it goes fast. If there is a box, everything works together to move the whole thing quickly.

sections.title: Addressing and Logical Channels
sections.content:
HYPERchannel addressing is hierarchical and flexible. An address has four parts: Domain (the highest level), Network (within a domain), Unit (the physical adapter), and Logical To (a port or process number). This allows the system to support networks with multiple domains and networks without changing the basic addressing scheme. For addresses outside the local domain and network, there is a special True Unit field for compatibility with earlier equipment.

The Logical To field serves a function similar to the protocol type field in Ethernet, but with a key difference: the logical TO address is part of the delivery mechanism itself. A process registers to receive all messages with a particular logical TO address, and the network hardware delivers messages based on this field. Multiple independent protocol stacks (such as two separate OSI implementations) can run on the same HYPERchannel interface by using different logical TO addresses. An Age Count field acts as a time-to-live, decremented each time a message crosses a bridge, to prevent packets from circulating endlessly in a misconfigured network.
sections.plainLanguage: The address tells the network where a message should go, like a mailing address on an envelope. The address also names which software program should receive it, like naming a person in the house. Several programs can share the same network connection by using different names.

sections.title: Broadcast Emulation for OSI Routing
sections.content:
HYPERchannel has no hardware broadcast capability; messages always go to a specific unit. However, ES-IS (End System to Intermediate System) and IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System) are OSI routing protocols that require broadcasting to discover neighbors. To work around this, systems maintain a list of known peers and manually send individual copies of broadcast packets to each one.

For ES-IS, end systems send Hello packets individually to every intermediate system they know about, spaced out over time to avoid overwhelming the network. Intermediate systems keep a complete list of other intermediate systems and send their own announcements to each one. When there are no real intermediate systems on the network, special nodes called SNAREs (SubNetwork Address Resolution Entities) emulate them: they act as address managers, learning which end systems exist, and forwarding traffic between them while sending redirect messages to inform end systems of the correct addresses to use.

For IS-IS, the approach is even simpler. Each intermediate system runs the IS-IS protocol normally but, whenever it needs to broadcast a message, it sends individual copies to every other IS on its list, spaced at least 0.1 seconds apart. This manual distribution is transparent to the IS-IS protocol itself and allows IS-IS to work despite the lack of hardware broadcast support.
sections.plainLanguage: The network does not let you yell to everyone at once. So when a system needs to tell everyone something, it sends the same message to each system one by one, with a pause between each one to keep things calm. This trick makes the protocols work even though the cable cannot broadcast.

sections.title: LLC1 Protocol Encapsulation
sections.content:
For OSI protocols to travel on HYPERchannel, they are wrapped in an LLC1 (Logical Link Control, type 1) header. This is an unnumbered, connectionless data link protocol. The RFC assigns the message type value 0x0B01 (bytes 8 and 9 of the HYPERchannel header) to identify LLC1 packets. A standardized protocol registry maintained by Network Systems Corporation ensures that different protocols do not collide.

The LLC1 header consists of three bytes: a destination Service Access Point (SAP), a source SAP, and a function code. For OSI CLNP traffic, both SAPs are set to 0xFE, and the function code is 0x03 for normal data. The LLC1 header sits at byte 16 of the HYPERchannel message proper, immediately after the delivery information. Higher-layer protocol data (such as CLNP, then transport, then application) follows directly. If the information fits in the message proper, no associated data is needed; otherwise, the payload flows into the associated data section.
sections.plainLanguage: To send an OSI message on HYPERchannel, you wrap it in an LLC1 label, which is three extra bytes that say who is sending, who should receive, and what kind of message it is. The HYPERchannel header then labels the whole thing with the number 0x0B01 so the equipment knows it is an LLC1 packet.
